“Time has gone by, but the scars will never ever be healed, and the fans will never ever forget,” he said. “So you can always rely on our supporters to be there for you when you need them.”

His report also cleared Liverpool fans of blame for the tragedy, after lurid tabloid headlines had provoked revulsion on Merseyside.

Prime Minister Gordon Brown referred to the controversy in an interview released on Liverpool’s official television channel.

In 2016, fresh inquests concluded that the victims were unlawfully killed and that errors by police and ambulance services contributed to the disaster. The jury also found that supporters’ behavior did not cause or contribute to the crush.

Those findings were seen in Liverpool as a landmark moment — an official vindication of what families and fans had said for years.

At this year’s commemorations, supporters again spoke of grief, resilience and justice. Many carried banners and scarves bearing the number 97, while others stood quietly by memorials honoring the victims. The message from the crowd remained familiar: the dead must be remembered, and those responsible must be held to account.

Hillsborough’s legacy continues to shape English football. The disaster transformed stadium safety, policing and crowd management, but it also left a lasting scar on Liverpool and its supporters.
